text: The PersistentVolume you built last lesson pointed at a disk that already existed in Azure, created by hand. That's fine for one lab PV. It falls apart once dozens of applications each need their own storage, because a human has to go create a real cloud disk through the Azure or AWS console before every single claim can bind. Dynamic provisioning removes that human step entirely.

The object that makes it possible is the StorageClass, and it isn't storage itself — it's closer to a recipe. It names a provisioner, the CSI driver that actually talks to the cloud, plus the parameters that provisioner should use. provisioner: disk.csi.azure.com is AKS's driver for Azure Disk; the AWS equivalent is ebs.csi.aws.com. reclaimPolicy: Retain decides whether the real disk survives after its PVC is deleted.

A PVC triggers all of this just by naming a storageClassName instead of waiting for a hand-created PV to match. The moment this PVC is created, disk.csi.azure.com calls the Azure API, provisions a brand-new managed disk at the requested size and tier, creates a matching PersistentVolume, and binds the two together — nobody ever opens the Azure portal, and no PV existed beforehand.

volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer adds one refinement worth knowing: instead of creating the disk the instant the PVC appears, it waits until a Pod actually using the claim gets scheduled, then provisions the disk in that same availability zone. Skip that, and a disk can get created somewhere the Pod's node can never reach, leaving it stuck attaching forever.

Most managed clusters ship with a default StorageClass already installed, marked with an is-default-class annotation, so a PVC that never mentions storageClassName at all still gets dynamically provisioned storage automatically. Run kubectl get storageclass on any new cluster before assuming you know what disk tier your Pods are about to receive — AKS's default and EKS's default are not the same thing.

So 'no storage class specified' never actually means 'no storage class used' — it means whichever one is marked default did the work quietly. With provisioning now fully automatic, the next question is what kind of workload actually needs its own dedicated, stable storage per replica, which is exactly where StatefulSets come in.
